result.abstractText:
Background

This study aimed to characterize the clinical and genetic features of a Chinese family with cone-rod dystrophy in which compound heterozygous PCDH15 variants were identified.

Methods

A Chinese pedigree with autosomal recessive cone-rod dystrophy was investigated. A comprehensive ophthalmic assessment was performed in the proband, a 42-year-old woman, together with genetic evaluation of her family members. Candidate variants were identified using whole-exome sequencing and subsequently assessed by Sanger sequencing and family segregation analysis.

Results

Ophthalmoscopic examination revealed pigmentary changes and atrophic lesions affecting the posterior pole and peripapillary area bilaterally. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) demonstrated bilateral outer retinal layer atrophy with disruption of the ellipsoid zone at the posterior pole. Multifocal electroretinography (mfERG) revealed attenuated central responses, while full-field electroretinography (ffERG) documented a more pronounced reduction in cone-mediated (photopic) responses. Two novel compound heterozygous variants in PCDH15, namely c.4903_4906del (p.Glu1635Lysfs*4) and c.3470C>A (p.Ala1157Glu), were identified in this autosomal recessive cone-rod dystrophy pedigree. Family co-segregation analysis provided supportive evidence for their potential association with the disease phenotype. Cross-species analysis revealed high evolutionary conservation of the PCDH15 protein. Three-dimensional structural modeling predicted potential alterations in protein structure.

Conclusion

To our knowledge, this is the first report describing an association between compound heterozygous PCDH15 variants and cone-rod dystrophy, thereby providing preliminary evidence that may broaden the mutational spectrum associated with this gene.

result.abstractText:
Background

Mutations in the cone-rod homeobox (CRX) gene cause dominantly inherited retinopathies with striking phenotypic variability. We define the clinical spectrum and molecular mechanism of a Class III CRX frameshift variant (c.590del, p.(Pro197Argfs*22); CRXP197Rfs) segregating in a four-generation family.

Materials and methods

Six family members underwent genetic testing by a retinal dystrophy panel with Sanger confirmation. Carriers received longitudinal phenotyping, including visual acuity, fundus autofluorescence, optical coherence tomography (OCT), and full-field electroretinography (ffERG). Variant function was assessed by rhodopsin-promoter reporter assays in HEK293 cells and Crx-/- mouse retinal explants.

Results

Three carriers shared the identical variant yet showed cone-rod dystrophy in variable severity and adult-onset ages. The proband developed progressive central vision loss, nyctalopia, outer-retinal atrophy, and reduced ffERG responses. Two carriers remained asymptomatic with preserved acuity and normal ffERG, exhibiting only mild outer nuclear layer thinning and abnormal autofluorescence. CRXP197Rfs lacked transactivation activity and suppressed wild-type CRX function in a dose-dependent manner.

Conclusions

CRXP197Rfs is a dominant-negative allele that produces cone-rod dystrophy with variable intrafamilial phenotypes. These findings caution against genotype-based prognostication and support mutant-allele knockdown with gene augmentation as therapeutic strategies.

result.abstractText: Pattern electroretinography (PERG) is a non-invasive test of macular and retinal ganglion cell function, but its low amplitude and inter-subject variability limit its diagnostic use. This study compares three representations of the transient PERG waveform for the detection of six retinal and optic nerve conditions - Birdshot chorioretinopathy, cone-rod dystrophy, hereditary optic atrophy, macular dystrophy, retinitis pigmentosa and Stargardt disease - against healthy controls, using the publicly available PERG-IOBA dataset. A total of 672 recordings from 336 examinations of 304 participants were preprocessed in six stages, and three representations were evaluated under one identical protocol: the raw 255-point amplitude-preserving waveform; 60 engineered clinical, spectral, wavelet and complexity descriptors; and a hybrid representation of 343 variables combining both, with multi-wavelet features from db4, sym2 and coif3. Performance was estimated by 10 × 5-fold participant-grouped cross-validation, in which both eyes and all repeat visits of an individual were kept in the same partition, with nested hyperparameter selection and all data-derived preprocessing fitted inside each training fold. Under the pre-specified primary classifier, the raw waveform gave the highest pooled out-of-fold AUC in four of the six classes (0.906 in cone-rod dystrophy, 0.842 in retinitis pigmentosa, 0.755 in macular dystrophy, 0.673 in hereditary optic atrophy) and the engineered descriptors in the remaining two (0.803 in Stargardt disease, 0.657 in Birdshot chorioretinopathy). The hybrid representation was highest in none, falling below the raw waveform in five of six classes by 0.002 to 0.018, and no non-linear classifier showed a hybrid advantage above 0.006 in mean AUC. A sensitivity analysis identified what does matter: removing the absolute amplitude scale by per-signal z-scoring cost the raw representation 0.055 AUC on average but the engineered descriptors only 0.023, and reversed the ordering of the three representations. Engineered descriptors did not improve on the waveform, but they made the problem tractable for linear models, which gained 0.128 in mean AUC from the reduction in dimensionality. These internally validated findings indicate that absolute PERG amplitude should be preserved rather than normalised away; participant-independent, multi-centre validation is required before clinical application.

result.abstractText:
Purpose

In this study, we present three patients diagnosed with rod-cone and cone-rod dystrophy carrying likely biallelic variants in UBAP1L.

Methods

In this cross-sectional study, three participants underwent ophthalmological examinations and genetic testing. The clinical examination included best-corrected visual acuity, kinetic perimetry, ultrawidefield fundus autofluorescence and pseudocolor photography optical coherence tomography and electrophysiology. Genetic diagnostic testing was performed by in silico inherited retinal disease (IRD) gene panel testing based on genome sequencing.

Results

Participant A showed a rod-cone dystrophy phenotype with myopia and a relatively late disease onset in the fourth decade. Participants B and C showed a cone-rod dystrophy phenotype. Genetic diagnostic testing revealed two heterozygous variants in UBAP1L in participant A, namely a 1 bp deletion c.566del, p.Ser189ThrfsTer80 and a variant in the consensus splice region c.910-7 G > A, p.?, an apparent homozygous 1 bp deletion c.472del, p.Ala158ArgfsTer27 in participant B, and a homozygous canonical splice-site variant c.120 + 1 G > T, p.? in participant C.

Conclusions

Three novel disease-associated variants and one previously reported variant in the UBAP1L gene were identified as the likely cause of rod-cone dystrophy and cone-rod dystrophy phenotypes. The identification of additional cases, together with detailed phenotypic characterization and longitudinal follow-up, will enable clearer genotype-phenotype correlations in the future.

result.abstractText:
Introduction

Retinitis pigmentosa GTPase regulator (RPGR) mutations are associated with X-linked inherited retinal diseases (IRDs), with variable phenotypes including retinitis pigmentosa (RP), cone-rod dystrophy (CRD), and cone dystrophy (CD). Tapetal-like reflex (TLR) is commonly observed in female carriers and has more recently been reported in hemizygous male patients with cone-dominant or cone-rod phenotypes. Here, we report two male patients with RPGR mutations and TLR.

Materials and methods

Clinical history, ophthalmic examination, multimodal retinal imaging, and genetic testing were reviewed in two unrelated Thai males with confirmed RPGR mutations.

Results

The first patient was a 9-year-old boy with sector RP and progressive bilateral blurred vision. The second was a 24-year-old man with sector RP and CD. Both exhibited a characteristic TLR at the posterior pole despite being affected males. These cases illustrate the phenotypic variability associated with RPGR mutations and the occurrence of TLR in affected males.

Conclusion

TLR may serve as a useful clinical clue to RPGR-related disease in both female carriers and affected males, including those with milder phenotypes such as sector RP. In affected males, the presence of TLR may be associated with preserved outer retinal structures and could indicate a milder phenotype, an earlier disease stage, or a more favorable prognosis.
